takes.why: Very playable this week even as the backup — Mike's start of the week against Denver.
takes.mechanism: Six yards per carry on 22 attempts, second only to Kenneth Walker among backs; Denver is dead last in EPA per rush and in yards after contact per attempt allowed and 29th in fantasy points allowed to RBs.

takes.why: Start him as the stack with Purdy against Arizona — he is the last man standing.
takes.mechanism: Lining up 50% out wide, 45% in the slot and 5% in the backfield, and with Kittle limited coming back Shanahan is out of other options in his 'this is how we win' script.

takes.why: Could not imagine benching him — he expects a billion points in the Buffalo game and a very fine fantasy week.
takes.mechanism: He barely practiced last week and was a decoy on under half the snaps, but is a full participant Wednesday; Buffalo is 31st in points per drive allowed, 28th in pass success rate allowed and 30th in fantasy points allowed to WRs, leaking specifically to slot receivers, and the Chargers desperately need him.

takes.why: Start him slightly over Matthew Golden, Ladd McConkey and Malik Nabers as a Nacua replacement — but he is behind Parker Washington as an asset.
takes.mechanism: He is healthier than McConkey, who may still be wearing a protective vest for a chest/rib injury.

takes.why: Start him — he looks like Buffalo's number one receiver even with DJ Moore on the field.
takes.mechanism: Always been excellent per route; now healthy after playing about 38% of snaps through a knee injury last year, he is finally running a full route load as the 25th overall pick.

takes.why: Trade DK Metcalf straight up for him and trade Josh Jacobs for him immediately.
takes.mechanism: In a tight-end premium format he is close to Tee Higgins as a top-50 rest-of-season asset.

takes.why: Start him over Harold Fannin, Kenyon Sadiq and Oronde Gadsden II, and roster him for the rest of the season — but behind Schultz, Terrance Ferguson and Jake Ferguson.
takes.mechanism: As good a touchdown bet as any tight end because he is enormous and always involved near the red zone; his snap counts are very low now and should rise as the season goes on.

takes.why: Not good enough to start — they take Waller over him even in the same game.
takes.mechanism: 17% target share through two weeks in a three-way Browns split with Boston and Concepcion.

takes.why: Dust — trade him straight up for Travis Kelce or Mark Andrews if anyone will do it.
takes.mechanism: Buried in a spread-out Browns target tree; the one upside path is Shedeur Sanders taking over and throwing shorter, quicker passes.

takes.why: Start him over Darren Waller — the touchdown odds are lower but the snaps are not.
takes.mechanism: Two touchdowns last week, he is on the field more than Waller and used between the twenties, and both can catch touchdowns; snaps break the tie.

takes.why: A secondary start of the week and a waiver add if Puka Nacua is out.
takes.mechanism: With Nacua inactive the Rams' targets redistribute to him; they rank him ahead of Waller, Sadiq and Gadsden this week.

takes.why: A bench stash and DFS play with a genuine breakout path this week, not a start over Waller or Ferguson.
takes.mechanism: Mason Taylor did not practice and looks out; Sadiq is a first-round pick with an off-the-charts athletic profile, and athletic testing matters at tight end more than at any other position — a first-rounder who produces while the starter is out simply takes the job.

takes.why: The moment to buy low is now — he should have a much better rest of season.
takes.mechanism: With Alec Pierce missing an extended period he benefits from target consolidation; he was a yards-after-catch machine in college and led all pass catchers in YAC through the first three weeks last season, and his YAC per catch has collapsed from 10.8 to 3.8, so the touchdowns are propping up tiny yardage totals.

takes.why: Start Pitts over Oronde Gadsden II — the projections are a wash (8.0 vs 8.2) so take the guy you know will be on the field.
takes.mechanism: Pitts runs routes tonight with Michael Penix and has upside; the Chargers signed Charlie Kolar and traded for David Njoku precisely because they don't trust Gadsden to block, so McDaniel can pull him in hurry-up situations.

takes.why: An okay desperation start — the injuries force him onto the field almost every play.
takes.mechanism: Njoku and Kolar are on IR, so he plays by default; he is not a complete tight end (athletic, free-releasing, non-blocker) and had a touchdown on only two targets last week.

takes.why: Mike starts him the moment he is active; Jason remains skeptical until he sees him play.
takes.mechanism: Limited participant Wednesday and again Thursday after missing time — practice trend is positive but the active designation is the gate.

takes.why: Start Brock Bowers over him and sell high on Kittle while you still can.
takes.mechanism: Coming off a big week while still recovering, and San Francisco cannot overload him — Deebo is the designed focal point this week.

takes.why: Start him — he was a start-of-the-week finalist and if he fails in this matchup there is no week you can play him.
takes.mechanism: Carolina is dead last in yards per carry allowed, rushing touchdowns allowed and EPA per rush this year, was bad last year and was one of the worst run defenses of all time the year before — a true run funnel; Cleveland are only two-point underdogs so the touchdown equity is there.

takes.why: Should be okay and playable if healthy — Mike would even start him over Judkins.
takes.mechanism: Running for 4.7 yards a carry and the Giants cannot stop running backs; volume went 7 carries in Week 1 to 14 in Week 2, but he and Tyjae Spears both missed Wednesday with ankles.

takes.why: A bench week — the talent is real but the environment is not.
takes.mechanism: A 24% target share that is 'the biggest slice of a turd pie' — Tennessee will not throw, he has not seen a single target 20-plus yards downfield all year, and the game has bad weather and the lowest over/under of the week (38.5).

takes.why: Playable this week — Mike would start him over DK Metcalf and over Denzel Boston.
takes.mechanism: He is ahead of Garrett Wilson in target share and the Detroit game environment (over has hit in six straight Lions games, 47.5 total) is far better than the Pittsburgh game.

takes.why: Keep starting him — volatility is the price of admission for a WR3/flex who wins you weeks.
takes.mechanism: Played 97% of snaps; a waiver receiver who reliably gives you seven to nine points cannot win a matchup, and Williams was drafted to go nuclear.

takes.why: A perfect buy-low — the right return when selling Rashee Rice or A.J. Brown.
takes.mechanism: Ranked above both of them on his rest-of-season list while the market treats him as a volatile flex.

takes.why: Andy would go back to the well this week; Mike would rather play Adonai Mitchell and avoid him.
takes.mechanism: The targets are there, but the Steelers offense is hard to watch and Cincinnati is a tough spot in a 42.5-total AFC North game.

takes.why: A floor-plus-touchdown play you could do worse than.
takes.mechanism: Cincinnati has been the tight-end funnel to attack for roughly eight straight years, and nobody else in Pittsburgh's passing game is a credible touchdown-scorer.

takes.why: Take the volume if he is alone in the backfield, but he is definitely still injured.
takes.mechanism: Back at practice but limited, while Rico Dowdle still has not practiced — a Warren-only backfield is the bull case.

takes.why: Worth half your FAAB in a standard 12-teamer — probably a discount — and a fair one-for-one return for Aaron Jones or Stefon Diggs.
takes.mechanism: His start-sit tool projects Warren at 14.7 points versus Aaron Jones at 12.7 for Week 3, pending whether Rico Dowdle plays.

takes.why: He wants one week where Warren and Dowdle are both out and the late-round rookie gets the full role.
takes.mechanism: An outrageously good college analytical profile and a jack-of-all-trades skill set; as good a receiver as he is a runner, a perfect Aaron Rodgers checkdown target the way Kenny Gainwell was last year.

takes.why: Andy's almost-upset pick is the Steelers, and the playable fantasy asset in that game is the defense.
takes.mechanism: Through two weeks Pittsburgh is first against quarterbacks, second against wide receivers and fifth against tight ends and will bring the pass rush — with the caveat that the two samples were Cooper Rush and a struggling Drake Maye; Jalen Ramsey's status is the swing factor.

takes.why: An easy start along with Higgins, Burrow and Chase Brown, but do not expect prolific numbers in Pittsburgh.
takes.mechanism: Cincinnati's offense has not clicked on all cylinders yet (the defense has carried them) and the Steelers' DNA is pass defense; low 42.5 total.

takes.why: No reason to trade a borderline top-five rest-of-season player just because you have injuries elsewhere.
takes.mechanism: He is roughly fifth overall on the rest-of-season list; two weeks is not a reason to move a cornerstone.

takes.why: Mike would start him over Jadarian Price, but the game environment is unexciting.
takes.mechanism: Seattle salted away the fourth quarter with Wilson after Price was hurt, and Washington was very bad against RBs last year; Seattle's 24-point implied total is fine but the game should disappear fast on few plays.

takes.why: Good news that he was seen in practice — he is in a good spot as a seven-point favorite.
takes.mechanism: Through three quarters last week Price had the carry lead; the fourth-quarter Wilson workload came after Price was knocked out.

takes.why: A sneaky start in a blowout spot — he could get ten carries in the fourth quarter alone.
takes.mechanism: The rookie has looked great behind Kenneth Walker and Kansas City is a 10.5-point road favorite with a 28.5-point implied total against Miami, so the fourth quarter is his.

takes.why: Stash him (and Kaelon Black) ahead of a better weekly projection like R.J. Harvey — the home-run outcome is what you are buying.
takes.mechanism: If Kenneth Walker or Christian McCaffrey gets hurt, the handcuff inherits a league-winning role; a bench player you won't start should be bought for contingency, not projection.

takes.why: A stash worth a bench spot over a startable-but-capped option.
takes.mechanism: Direct contingency on Christian McCaffrey's workload; contingent upside beats a flex projection for a bench slot.

takes.why: The number-one waiver pickup in about half of leagues did not practice — they withdrew a Denver-backfield claim over it.
takes.mechanism: Official Wednesday report has Coleman as did-not-participate while J.K. Dobbins and R.J. Harvey were limited, so the two players he was supposed to replace practiced more than he did.

takes.why: Avoid the entire Denver backfield right now.
takes.mechanism: Coleman looked like the clear add early in the week but is not practicing with an ankle injury, while Dobbins and Harvey are both practicing on hamstrings — a three-way gross split.

takes.why: If Aaron Jones is out, Mike would start Claiborne over DeeJay Dallas for the explosive upside even though Dallas likely plays more.
takes.mechanism: Great speed and a good system fit; Andy counters that the team does not trust him and Dallas is the more trusted, higher-snap player.

takes.why: The more trusted Minnesota back who will play more snaps if Aaron Jones sits.
takes.mechanism: Signed midweek to the active roster and already ahead of the rookie in the coaching staff's trust hierarchy; Andy expects him to get more work regardless.

takes.why: His 31st-ranked rest-of-season player and a top-25 asset — buy him off the down week, and anyone trading Achane, Tuten or Tee Higgins for him is losing the deal.
takes.mechanism: Ranked far above both Achane (30th is not the same tier once you account for redraft cost) and Bhayshul Tuten (barely top-50); the Caleb Williams absence is a fair concern but priced in.

takes.why: Anyone who traded D'Andre Swift for Tuten fumbled the bag — he is barely a top-50 rest-of-season player.
takes.mechanism: Swift is a top-25 rest-of-season asset; the backfield-share argument for Tuten does not close a gap that large.

takes.why: Flex him slightly over D'Andre Swift this week; as an asset he is only around the 30th-ranked player.
takes.mechanism: Swift faces the Eagles' defensive line on Monday night without Caleb Williams and possibly with a third-string quarterback, in a game both teams may want to grind out.

takes.why: A nothing burger in any trade — do not pay for him, and trade him for Dalton Kincaid immediately if you own him.
takes.mechanism: On the commissioner's exempt list facing a possible four-to-six-game suspension with the missed games already counting, so he may not play until Week 7; he will return out of football shape after a camp groin injury behind horrendous Packers run blocking.

takes.why: Still his number-two overall player rest of season and matchup-proof — trade Saquon Barkley plus Zay Flowers, or Javonte Williams plus Breece Hall, for him instantly.
takes.mechanism: A guaranteed 20-to-30 points a week; his ordinal list puts only Gibbs ahead, with Jonathan Taylor and Kenneth Walker behind.

takes.why: A top-five rest-of-season player — do not trade him, and do not overpay to get him this early.
takes.mechanism: Nobody is moving him except for Gibbs-tier value; if you are offered Walker plus JSN for Gibbs, take it instantly.

takes.why: He is back to being a fantasy superstar — start him.
takes.mechanism: Two reasons: Kenneth Walker III giving the offense a real run game, and Matt Nagy no longer calling plays — Mahomes finished 1, 4, 4, 1 at QB before Nagy and 8, 11, 11 with him.

takes.why: Start him on Thursday night over Deshaun Watson and Marcus Mariota.
takes.mechanism: The Packers' defense is suspect: pressuring and blitzing a lot over a two-week sample, which should open the offense up.

takes.why: They do not believe he fixes everything for the Falcons, even though many managers will sneak him in expecting an unlock.
takes.mechanism: Atlanta brought Tua Tagovailoa in to replace him and Tua looked worse in preseason; Penix was medically cleared over a week ago and said he wasn't ready.

takes.why: Start him Thursday and he is a top-24 rest-of-season asset — take London over Tee Higgins, and take him for Nabers instantly.
takes.mechanism: The matchup is tougher than Golden's because Green Bay will put help over the top on the number-one receiver, but the volume and rank hold.

takes.why: Start him Thursday night (and Stroud alongside him in two-QB lineups).
takes.mechanism: A quality streaming-tier quarterback available off waivers; Sal owns him in his home league for the Thursday game.

takes.why: Whatever Miami paid for, they are not using it — the offense is broken.
takes.mechanism: Kirk Cousins has more rushing attempts than Willis on the year; he had six rushes for 39 yards in Week 1 and almost nothing since, and a pocket-passing Willis with a rookie receiver room is pointless.

takes.why: Only startable in a two-point-per-reception or point-per-target format — he should lead Miami in targets.
takes.mechanism: Volume by default with Caleb Douglas hurt, but the Dolphins' offense caps the ceiling entirely.

takes.why: Worth rostering in a 12-team league and probably their stream of the week in Week 4 — but not startable against Seattle.
takes.mechanism: He started eight games last year averaging 11 fantasy points but with real spike weeks (23.3 against Denver), and the upcoming schedule (Indianapolis, then the Giants) is soft.

takes.why: They will not start any Washington player, White included.
takes.mechanism: Lowest implied team total of the week at 16.8 points with a backup quarterback against an elite Seattle defense.

takes.why: An obvious start against Washington.
takes.mechanism: Seattle is implied for 24 points and he is the concentrated target earner; the rest of the Seahawks' passing game is not startable.

takes.why: He is on the team because of injuries, not play.
takes.mechanism: Two drops hit him in the chest, which is abnormal for him, and his three-game suspension has been pushed — likely to land after court proceedings, probably after the season.

takes.why: Not confidently startable — neither is Xavier Hutchinson or Jared Wayne.
takes.mechanism: With Nico Collins not practicing, Houston's passing game is consolidated into Schultz and Montgomery and you cannot predict where the ball goes among the remaining receivers.

takes.why: Risky at best this week.
takes.mechanism: Dalton Kincaid has emerged as the de facto number-one receiver and DJ Moore may return, squeezing the rest of the room.

takes.why: Risky at best — a speculative add rather than a start.
takes.mechanism: Did not practice Wednesday immediately after his one confident receiving game.

takes.why: Probably play him if he is active, understanding the re-injury risk.
takes.mechanism: Limited on Wednesday, which is a good sign, but a hard fall on the shoulder could cost him again.

takes.why: Play Allen and Cook — Buffalo's offense is on fire.
takes.mechanism: Buffalo is 2-0, minus-7 at home with a 50.5 total, and Joe Brady has the offense on lock even as the defense looks suspect.

takes.why: A great play in a great matchup at Buffalo.
takes.mechanism: Buffalo's defense has been very bad (31st in points per drive allowed) and the Chargers should have to move the ball; getting McConkey back makes the whole offense function.

takes.why: You do not have to start him — two of three hosts now rank Bryce Young ahead of him.
takes.mechanism: He scored 7.9 fantasy points against the Raiders and the Chargers' offense has been broken without Ladd McConkey; Andy's counter is that targeting the Bills' defense with any piece is the play.

takes.why: Limited but trending to play; if he is downgraded, Mike prefers Kendre Miller over Alvin Kamara as the replacement.
takes.mechanism: Limited Wednesday with a hamstring despite getting no work; Andy expects Kamara to absorb one-yard passes if Etienne sits.

takes.why: The better option than Alvin Kamara if Travis Etienne is downgraded.
takes.mechanism: Kamara's role would be checkdowns, not volume; Miller inherits the actual carries.

takes.why: Not worried about the Wednesday absence — worry about Thursday and Friday.
takes.mechanism: Did not practice Wednesday and they expect San Francisco to take it easy with him; Purdy is startable regardless.

takes.why: Still holding hope — keep rolling him out and start him over Kenyon Sadiq all day; he would not trade Loveland plus Marvin Harrison Jr. for Kraft plus Tuten unless the price improves.
takes.mechanism: He is not selling a young starting tight end into a bad-week trough; the Chicago passing game should improve.

takes.why: Trade Josh Downs for him — yes; and Chase Brown for Breece Hall plus Love is a deal he'd make.
takes.mechanism: Ranked comparably to Javonte Williams rest of season while being acquirable at a receiver's price.

takes.why: Too valuable to move — a top-15 rest-of-season workhorse who wins his side of nearly every offered package.
takes.mechanism: Workhorse volume keeps his rest-of-season value above the Bucky Irving / Parker Washington tier even after a down game.

takes.why: A fine return for A.J. Brown, and worth Jaylen Warren plus Denzel Boston if you can get it done.
takes.mechanism: Ranked above A.J. Brown on the rest-of-season list while Brown misses six-plus weeks.

takes.why: Buy him through the absence — much better rest of season than Achane or Hubbard; swap either for him.
takes.mechanism: He did not practice and will miss this week but Sal expects him back in Week 4, so the discount is one game long.

takes.why: Very concerned — trade Saquon plus Zay Flowers for Bijan Robinson instantly, and he'd rather have Lamar Jackson plus D'Andre Swift than Purdy plus Saquon.
takes.mechanism: Not the injury but the offensive line; he is limited with a stinger and unlikely to play Week 3, and would only be a third-round pick if redrafting today.

takes.why: Not cooked, but capped — a weekly top-15 quarterback, not the top-five arm you drafted.
takes.mechanism: With A.J. Brown out and Diggs gone, nobody in New England's passing game creates explosive plays: Kyle Williams could but isn't playing, and DeMario Douglas, Hunter Henry and Mack Collins don't generate 20-plus-yard gains — the ceiling now depends on Maye's legs.

takes.why: The one Patriot who can create explosive plays — and he is not getting any run.
takes.mechanism: Named as the answer to New England's explosive-play problem, gated entirely by playing time.

takes.why: His WR30 this week, a slight start over Adonai Mitchell (WR32).
takes.mechanism: Remains inconsistent and has not been the deep threat Kansas City drafted him to be, but the blowout game environment supports the volume.

takes.why: A borderline waiver player — only add him over a non-playing stash like Caleb Douglas.
takes.mechanism: Appears at the bottom of the targets-per-route-run chart alongside Cooper Kupp as a washed player.

takes.why: A clear add over Chris Bell — drop the Miami rookie for him.
takes.mechanism: Free agent in the asker's league with real weekly startability versus a Dolphins rookie with no role.

takes.why: A deep-league stash only — and only if he would actually crack your lineup with Pollard and Spears out.
takes.mechanism: An exciting but flawed college player at Penn State; Pollard got a limited practice in Thursday, so the path likely does not open.

takes.why: A buy-low worth sending Rashee Rice or A.J. Brown for, and an acceptable secondary piece in a Henderson trade.
takes.mechanism: Ranked above the players he'd sell on the rest-of-season list while the market prices him off a slow start.

takes.why: An interesting return in a TreVeyon Henderson package, and one of the names above A.J. Brown he'd accept.
takes.mechanism: Rest-of-season rank above the players being sold; not a name he'd chase at full price.

takes.why: A solid one-for-one target for Aaron Jones — but droppable for Jameson Williams in shallow lineups.
takes.mechanism: Perceived value is depressed after a slow start while Aaron Jones' is inflated by one 23-touch game.

takes.why: A fair one-for-one for Aaron Jones right now.
takes.mechanism: Ranked above Jones (93rd) on the rest-of-season list while nobody in the market is high on him.

takes.why: Keep him rather than swapping for Kenyon Sadiq or Kenny Gainwell — those are waiver-tier names.
takes.mechanism: No upgrade in trading one waiver asset for another; Sadiq may be on waivers again next week.

takes.why: Take Marks over Keaton Mitchell in a trade, but do not start him over Travis Etienne.
takes.mechanism: Still being out-snapped by David Montgomery, so he is a bench asset with efficiency, not a starter.

takes.why: A top-five rest-of-season player — always take the JT side of a trade.
takes.mechanism: One of only five backs to finish top-12 in both weeks; his ordinal list has him behind only Gibbs and Bijan among RBs.

takes.why: The right return when selling Malik Nabers, and he would rather have Higgins than Mike Evans straight up — but not over Drake London.
takes.mechanism: Rest-of-season ordinal places him above Nabers (32nd) and Evans, below London (21st).

takes.why: Overall RB1 for week 3 and one of three elite backs Sal expects a two-plus-touchdown game from.
takes.mechanism: Detroit is a 6.5-point favorite with a 27-point implied team total, which pushes his projection to 25.8 PPR points; elite RBs in high team totals with favorite game scripts get the goal-line volume.

takes.why: RB2 on the week and a projected 20-plus-point game.
takes.mechanism: Kansas City is a 10.5-point favorite against Miami with a 28-point team total, the classic script for volume plus red-zone work.

takes.why: RB3 with a 20-plus-point projection, and Sal is explicitly not panicking about the week-2 snap split.
takes.mechanism: 28-point team total as an 8.5-point favorite; his week-2 55% snap share and 45% rush-attempt share came in a blowout where there was no reason to give him ten more pointless touches.

takes.why: Automatic start in the highest-total game on the slate and a likely touchdown.
takes.mechanism: Roughly a 52-point game total against a Dallas defense that was bad against the run all of last year and again in week 1.

takes.why: RB5 despite a weak team environment, and the Footballers also say play him.
takes.mechanism: Insane workhorse usage carries him even at a 20.5-point team total as a 3-point underdog; Brock Bowers' return pulls extra bodies out of the box, and the Saints have allowed 26.2 fantasy points per game to RBs.

takes.why: RB6 and a must start whose matchup grades NEUTRAL rather than difficult despite Houston's run-defense rank.
takes.mechanism: Houston is a top-6 run defense but is struggling to tackle, the Colts have the 9th-ranked offensive line, and Taylor's pass-game usage makes him game-flow independent for the first time in his career.

takes.why: Ranked RB7 in a make-or-break week Sal admits he could be talked down from.
takes.mechanism: Miami is a 10.5-point underdog with only a 17.5-point team total, but if the Dolphins finally throw when trailing he projects to roughly five catches, which is 18.8 PPR points; he already gets every important touch (25 opportunities last week).

takes.why: RB8 on a clean game-script projection.
takes.mechanism: Buffalo is a 7.5-point favorite against the Chargers, which is a good game script for an early-down back.

takes.why: Still RB9 this week but Sal flags a rest-of-season concern about his passing-game usage.
takes.mechanism: Most of his upside the last two years came from checkdowns while trailing; the Bengals defense has improved through two weeks and they face a weak Steelers offense, so Cincinnati may not have to play from behind.

takes.why: Must-start top-10 back this week, which Sal says will not be true most weeks.
takes.mechanism: Second-best matchup on the entire slate: Cleveland ranks 28th of 32 against the run and bottom-10 in tackling with no Myles Garrett, while Carolina has the 6th-ranked run-blocking unit.

takes.why: Rest of season the Footballers would trade Hubbard away for Jeremiyah Love even after three straight top-12 weeks.
takes.mechanism: None stated beyond the relative upside of Love's eventual bell-cow role; Hubbard's value is treated as already realized.

takes.why: Top-12 back IF he plays Monday night, pending the Thursday practice report.
takes.mechanism: Philadelphia should play with a big lead against a bad Bears team potentially starting a third-string quarterback, which gets him 16-plus opportunities.

takes.why: Must start; his week-2 usage is vintage Bucky from the second half of his rookie year.
takes.mechanism: 77% of snaps, 81% of rush attempts, 54% of routes run with no Sean Tucker involved.

takes.why: Start him for the volume but expect a bad game and hope for a touchdown.
takes.mechanism: The feared 50/50 split with Kenny Gainwell has already been answered (15 and 21 opportunities), but the Minnesota defense has been outrageously good and the game total is only 42.5.

takes.why: Must start in what Sal calls a fantasy wonderland for the entire Cowboys offense.
takes.mechanism: Dallas is a 3.5-point underdog but still projected for 24 points, meaning Dak throws 40-plus times; Javonte gets three or four catches plus all the goal-line and red-zone work, and held over 80% of snaps even in a bad week.

takes.why: Do not let the long-term concern talk push him out of your lineup; he is the workhorse right now.
takes.mechanism: Nobody on the roster is coming to take the job while Jonathan Brooks is out six weeks; the real long-term threat named is AJ Dillon, not Brooks.

takes.why: RB14 but entirely dependent on the injury report.
takes.mechanism: Knee injury on Wednesday and he turns 32 soon; if he is out the backfield is an unplayable mess.

takes.why: A must-start top-15 back if Rico Dowdle is out, projected 13.2 PPR points.
takes.mechanism: Pittsburgh is a 3.5-point underdog and Aaron Rodgers leads the NFL in pass attempts, so Warren gets significant checkdown targets against a Bengals defense that has been good downfield.

takes.why: RB16 and an automatic start; the Braelon Allen touchdown did not change the split.
takes.mechanism: Week 2: 70% of rush attempts, 43% of routes, 65% of snaps plus a 40-plus-yard receiving explosive; Gino Smith likes targeting him and the Jets project to play from behind as 6.5-point underdogs.

takes.why: RB17 in a good matchup, with the Jaxson Dart injury actually helping him.
takes.mechanism: No Dart means more red-zone rushing upside for Skattebo, provided Jameis Winston plays like his 2025 fill-in self; the Footballers add that rain is now forecast for this game, which hurts the passing side and helps the run.

takes.why: RB18, well below the top-10 ceiling drafters paid for.
takes.mechanism: 7.5-point underdog in a Chargers offense that does not look good, Ladd McConkey likely not 100%, and both blocking tight ends (Kolar, Njoku) are banged up.

takes.why: RB19 and a sketchy spot despite a surface-level favorable matchup.
takes.mechanism: The matchups guide grades Philadelphia's front favorably on two weeks of data, but with no Caleb Williams and Case Keenum starting, the Eagles have even more reason to load the box, which the two-week sample does not account for.

takes.why: RB20 this week only; Sal does not like him rest of season.
takes.mechanism: 2.5-point favorite in a good matchup against the Colts, which is the spot for him to get back into the end zone.

takes.why: Startable at RB21 but Sal does not love it.
takes.mechanism: Cleveland is only a 2.5-point underdog so the game should stay close, and close games plus a decent matchup are the only script in which he produces; he did nothing on the ground even in last week's win.

takes.why: RB22 but Sal says RB18 is a fine argument.
takes.mechanism: Tougher matchup against Denver; he still held 56% of snaps and 45% of routes last week even after fumbling.

takes.why: RB23 now, with the unlock coming soon rather than this week.
takes.mechanism: He already leads the backfield in carries (56% on only 40% of snaps) but Allgeier owns the routes (55%) despite being slow as a receiver; Love is six weeks removed from the high ankle sprain and the route share is what flips.

takes.why: The headline buy-low of the week; they would trade Chuba Hubbard for him straight up even after three straight top-12 Hubbard weeks.
takes.mechanism: They expect Love to reach 60% of the backfield opportunities, which is the Bijan/Allgeier template; the market has already discounted him (58.5 scrimmage-yard prop versus just under 100 for McCaffrey), and the takeover could be this week with a divisional game and a hurting 49ers defensive line.

takes.why: Breakout candidate and a top-24 back whose 49% snap share badly understates the role.
takes.mechanism: 54% of rush attempts, team lead in routes run, and the goal-line/red-zone wildcat package (scored on it); Chris Rodriguez has fallen to a clear backup and is a drop in 10- and 12-team formats.

takes.why: He is the dude in Jacksonville; the decision has been made.
takes.mechanism: Chris Rodriguez has only six opportunities in each of the last two weeks and got dumped in the Footballers' league of record.

takes.why: Hangs on at RB25 but is a borderline bench player; if it does not happen this week it never will.
takes.mechanism: Amazing matchup as favorites against the Raiders on a high-play-volume Saints offense is the best environment he will get all year.

takes.why: RB26 and a flex option at best.
takes.mechanism: Coming off a fumble, he goes back to splitting the backfield with TreVeyon Henderson.

takes.why: Impossible to trust week to week; Mike would still play Stevenson over him despite the fumble.
takes.mechanism: He played 60% of snaps with 16 carries but ZERO targets and zero receptions, so his only path to a useful score is a special run; they expect screens to come eventually but the game script was a blowout.

takes.why: RB27, a flex option only in a double-flex league.
takes.mechanism: Underdog against the Giants, Tyjae Spears still involved, and there is no pass-catching upside even though Cam Ward played his best game last week.

takes.why: A sneaky start at RB29 ONLY if Jadarian Price is out or severely limited, despite Sal saying he does not think Wilson is all that talented.
takes.mechanism: Third-best matchup on the slate: Seattle is a 7-point favorite with a 24-point total, Washington ranks 29th against the run and bottom-10 in tackling, Seattle has a top-10 offensive line; 14-16 carries plus red-zone work if Price sits. His week-2 42% snap / 53% carry share is skewed because Price left a blowout.

takes.why: The Denver back Sal would start, but only if Dobbins and/or Jonah Coleman are out.
takes.mechanism: If all three backs are active he will not start any of them against the Rams; Dobbins and Harvey practiced limited with hamstrings while Coleman is the one not practicing.

takes.why: RB32 and a drop in a lot of 12-team formats.
takes.mechanism: Seven-point underdog without Jayden Daniels, so the only upside is checkdowns from a mobile Marcus Mariota who does not need them.

takes.why: Explicitly NOT a drop and a pretty solid play for the RB33 range.
takes.mechanism: Two-point favorite on a good offense gets him 8-12 carries; the camp reporting that Kyren keeps the passing work held (Kyren 45% of routes, Corum 21%) but the carries split 50/50 last week.

takes.why: Mike's Start of the Week, and he is playing both Corum and Kyren.

strategy_notes.note: Off-field/suspension risk to an incumbent is a legitimate accelerant for a rookie's snap timeline [FF]: the day-2/day-3 rookie WR base rate (slow starts, second-half relevance) can be overridden when the player ahead of him is under league investigation or otherwise unlikely to be part of the team's future — the org starts developing the rookie sooner. Check the incumbent's status, not just the rookie's draft capital.

Sanctioned buy conditions for a 30+ receiver [Sal]: he normally avoids aging WRs, but names the exact conjunction that overrides it — (a) the target competition in the room has been vacated, (b) a real QB upgrade arrived, and (c) the ADP has already fallen for the age/injury narrative. All three must hold (A.J. Brown, McLaurin, Evans); efficiency stats that survived the down year (YPRR, first downs per route run, zero drops) are the confirmation that the skills, not the situation, are intact.

Four to six games is the read-the-team threshold [FF]: the hosts converge on refusing to judge a team before week 4 and making the call by weeks 4-6 — early enough to still act before the fantasy playoffs, late enough that schedule strength has evened out. They validate the rule against prior-year week-4 standings (Baltimore 1-3, Arizona 2-2 and never winning again) rather than asserting it.

Price an injury backup against the real starter tiers, not the hype [FF]: when a starter goes down and his backup's ADP spikes, ask where the backup would rank if you KNEW he was starting — put him next to the actual committee starters (Tuten, Price, Warren, Stevenson) and see whether you would take him over any of them. That anchor exposed a pick-37 ADP on a day-3 back with no college production on a low-scoring offense. Pair it with the combine-vs-production check (an A.J. Dillon profile: elite athletic testing that never produced in college).

Do not double- and triple-count a risk that is already in the price [Sal]: for aging or injury-prone veterans, age, injury history and a current camp tightness report are often the same risk restated three ways. Once the ADP has fallen to reflect the known profile, an additional narrative ('everybody on that team gets hurt') is not new information and should not produce a further discount. The test is whether the report changes the week-1 availability branch — 25 days to heal with 'not considered serious' does not.

Stale-ADP trap on news-flip players [FF]: an ADP formed during a player's bad-news window (Nabers' ACL recovery pessimism) is already obsolete the moment the news flips, and every manager in the room is staring at that same number hoping for the steal. Never plan a build around the printed ADP of a player whose situation just improved — assume he goes a full round or more earlier than the number says.

Price a stack by naming the players you pass on [FF]: before drafting a stack partner, pull the platform ADP for that exact pick and say out loud who else is on the board. If the opportunity cost is real (DJ Moore in the late fifth costs Jameson Williams / Luther Burden / Tuten / Price), do not force the stack — either wait for a later round where he is free or switch to a cheaper correlated piece (the late-round TE version of the same stack).

Camp reception counts by quarterback as a target-pecking-order proxy [FF]: they explicitly want, for every team, the full ordered list of how many catches each pass catcher made from the starting QB across training camp — and treat that ordering as real signal while dismissing preseason completion percentage as noise ('they should be failing in preseason'). It is a usage metric available before any snap chart exists, and it resolved their New England pecking order (Brown > Doubs > Stevenson > Douglas > Henry > Boutte).

Three-outcome (wild-card) classification and its roster cap [FF]: sort picks into 'guaranteed to produce on some level' vs wild cards whose range genuinely spans worthless / flex-worthy / league-winning, and deliberately carry only one or two wild cards on a roster — 'you really don't want a bunch of those'. The classification is also a filter for hype: a player who cannot plausibly reach the league-winning end (Bucky Irving with the pass-catching role gone, R.J. Harvey behind two names) does not belong in the bucket regardless of how exciting he is.
Anchor with elite RBs: two RBs in your first three picks (reliability, not breakout swings) — RBs fly early this year and the position is barren by round 5.

The RB dead zone is back — RB24 now costs a 5th-round pick (a 7th in 2024) — grab two elite backs in the first 3-4 rounds and refuse to pay for middling RB2/3s (Etienne, Montgomery, Warren, Pollard all priced above projection).
Elite QB prices are the cheapest in years — Lamar a full round-plus cheaper than last year's QB2; Burrow (rd 5) / Daniels and Hurts (rd 6) are legitimate value even for late-round-QB drafters.
Wait on QB in 1QB: Allen is the lone QB priced in round 2 while Daniels/Hurts/Maye deliver comparable upside ~50 picks later; rounds 10-11 are the last window for Kyler/Mahomes/Purdy types.
Avoid RBs on bad teams: backs on sub-7-win teams hit ADP only ~30% of the time; 2026 teams that are underdogs in 3+ of their first 4 (ARI, CLE, IND, LV, MIA, NYJ, DEN) create uphill starts.
Don't stash day-2/3 rookie WRs early (48%/30% snaps, 2-4 targets through week 6) — only first-round rookies start day one; spend late picks on backup RBs whose value transfers predictably.

The old-WR cliff is the worst bet on the board: the 10 oldest drafted players beat ADP just 30% of the time and old WRs only 21% — this year that's Adams and Evans — with encore-effect exceptions (Henry, Kelce, Stafford).

Tight end is elite-or-punt: pay for Bowers/McBride/Loveland/Warren or wait for late profiles with 17%+ target share and 15%+ air-yard share (Likely, Goedert, Kincaid, Juwan Johnson) — mid-round TEs waste RB/WR upside picks.

Middle-round RB and middle-round TE are the two worst-priced blocks on the 2026 board [FF/Jason] — 'the opportunity cost is too great' there this year. The paired swing: late-round QB has gone so far out of fashion that QBs are falling past their value, so the current edge is the middle-round QB, not the last-round one. Strategy rotates every couple of years as ADP self-corrects; the job is to find whichever block the market has mispriced THIS season, not to re-run last year's rule.

Sleeper-definition inflation [FF]. With ADP now accurate front-to-back and the average manager far more informed, a genuine sleeper can no longer be a known player at a modest discount — it has to be a player where 'right now it seems impossible' and the honest base rate is near-total failure. Corollary they apply on the same breath: late-round shots must go to players you believe are actually GOOD, because 'there are late-round guys who just stink' and opportunity alone on a bad player is a wasted ticket. This is the same bar our league_winners screen enforces.

Dynasty horizon is three years, not ten [FF]. They rejected their own 10-year 'who would you take' question on principle: player trajectories are not forecastable past ~3 years, so dynasty value should be argued on a three-year window. Directly relevant to our never-cut-youth rule — a young stash's thesis should be defensible inside three seasons, not on an indefinite 'someday'.
Never put an early-week (Wed/Thu) player in a FLEX slot; put him in his positional slot so the flex stays open to cover Sunday injuries or news.

Kicker selection: prefer a good kicker on a mediocre offense that settles for 40-60 yard field goals and rarely goes for it on 4th down; avoid kickers on aggressive TD-heavy offenses (DET, LAR, DAL) even if they're better real-life kickers.
Use Vegas player props (reception O/U) as a trustworthy read on a player's expected Week-1 usage; big money keeps those lines tight.
When a team refuses to say where a player's 'soreness' is, read it as PR cover for the previously injured joint (e.g. the knee for a two-time ACL back) — a red flag, not noise.
The days before Week 1 are the peak sell-high window for camp-hype players: benchmark offers against real trades happening in other leagues that week and convert hype into proven target-earners.
Draft capital a team spends to acquire a player reveals its valuation: a 2028 6th-rounder for Kaleb Johnson means RB3, not a real competitor.
Explosive-play seasons regress: 1,000 yards on ~84 targets (18% share) is not repeatable; target share is the sustainable driver (Saquon's 2024-to-2025 as the RB analogue).
A bad offensive line hits inexperienced running backs first; check consensus O-line rankings before buying a new RB1.
Historical base rate: no NFL running back has returned productive from back-to-back ACL tears; lean on the history rather than betting against it.
A QB returning from an Achilles loses downfield power (Cousins, Rodgers precedents), which specifically hurts his deep-threat WR while pushing volume to short-area TE/RB options.
A bottom-5 offense craters even elite-talent pass catchers (ARI 2025 with McBride/Harrison); QB situation can turn a 2nd-round WR into 5th-round value.
New-regime discount: a coaching staff with no draft-capital or money attachment to a player (Skattebo, 4th-round pick) will not force-feed him; check who the new staff signed.
Week 1 for last-round stashes is a usage read, not a points read: track snap share (75%+ = full starter), routes and targets, then either punt them on the first waiver wire or hold with conviction.

Depth-chart order does not predict who takes over after an injury; evaluate the more talented backup (Ollie Gordon over Jaylen Wright, Jonah Coleman over RJ Harvey, Vidal behind Hampton) rather than the listed RB2.

Prefer insurance backs with standalone weekly touches (Corum, Brooks, C-Rod, Monangai, Allgeier, Gainwell) over pure handcuffs; early-season handcuffs with zero standalone value cost you waiver churn.
Only ~24% of top-24 RBs survive 17 weeks — plan on injuries at RB and size handcuff/FAAB accordingly; but don't full-FAAB a backup on a bad offense (Miami) because he won't be a top-10 RB anyway.
Rookie WR base rate: non-high-first-round rookies start slow; only stash the ones projected for 75%+ snaps from Week 1.

TE age curve differs from RB/WR: tight ends are routinely fine at 31-33 (especially TD-dependent ones) without being Hall of Famers; athleticism matters more at TE than any position and TE breakouts often take 4-6 years.
Update conclusions when the data changes (court date moved two months = shorter absence); don't hold a take after its premise moves.
Last-pick IR trick: draft an IR-eligible player (Pacheco, Tyson) with the final pick, move him to IR, and add a free flier — an extra roster spot for nothing.
Week 1 tiebreakers: defenses are ahead of offenses so expect low totals; home favorites get the RB start/sit nod in coin flips; don't overreact to Week 1 results.
Ignore platform Week-1 projections and draft grades: platforms exist to run leagues, not to project players; historically an A grade is a warning and a D/F often means a great team.

Off-field/discipline risk in dynasty: discount a player whose value is team-specific (Rashee Rice) more than one whose skill translates anywhere (Nacua) — the latter gets paid by a WR-needy team even if his current team walks.
Players on the commissioner's exempt list can't go to IR — the stash costs a real bench spot for as long as the case runs.

Saquon Barkley left Week 2 on the first snap, returned for about 12 second-half snaps wearing a neck protector, and finished with 4 carries for 9 yards; he did not speak to media, said he was okay, and had an MRI scheduled — best case a stinger, worst case a disc herniation.
Saquon Barkley ranks top-six in the NFL in rushing yards over expected through two games, essentially all of it earned in Week 1.
Bears Week 2 (a 9-3 game in atrocious weather): Rome Odunze 3-43 on 90% of routes (up from 53% in Week 1), Luther Burden III 3-32, Colston Loveland 1-3, Kalif Raymond 5-40.
Through two weeks Kalif Raymond leads the Bears with 13 catches while Rome Odunze, Luther Burden III and Colston Loveland have 14 catches combined.
Rhamondre Stevenson has 18 fumbles since 2021, the most of any NFL running back (PFF).

Week 2 New England backfield: Rhamondre Stevenson 6 carries for 43 yards on 36% of snaps; TreVeyon Henderson 16 carries including a 76-yard touchdown on 60% of snaps. After Stevenson's fumble, Henderson took 76% of carries to Stevenson's 24%.
New England's schedule after Week 3 at Jacksonville: Bills, Raiders, Bears and Dolphins in four of the next five — all softer run matchups.
George Pickens had a 26% target share on 81% of routes in Week 2 and sits at a 21% target share on the season, slightly ahead of his 21% mark from last year.
George Pickens has gone four consecutive games without a touchdown dating to last season — his longest drought since 2024 in Pittsburgh, when he was scoreless in five of six.
Dak Prescott's Week 2: 80% completions, 279 passing yards, 4 touchdowns, 0 interceptions; CeeDee Lamb went 8-153-2 and has 3 touchdowns through two games.

Arizona Week 2 backfield: Jeremiyah Love 9 carries for 29 yards on under 40% of snaps and 26% of routes; Tyler Allgeier 5 carries, led the team in snaps, ran 58% of routes. Jacoby Brissett threw 28 times for 95 yards.
Marvin Harrison Jr. through two weeks: 1 catch on 4 targets, 62 routes run, 33 receiving yards, one drop, no touchdowns, 4.3 PPR fantasy points.
Marvin Harrison Jr. ran 89% of routes in Week 2 but earned only a 7% target share (6% of his routes targeted); Kendrick Bourne led the team at 20% of routes with a 19% target share.
Marvin Harrison Jr. has been targeted on 6.9% of his routes this season; among 90 WRs with 30+ routes run, only Bryce Lance, Jakobi Meyers and Calvin Ridley are worse.

Houston Week 2 backfield: David Montgomery 6 carries for 10 yards (1.7 YPC), 43% of carries, 3% target share; Woody Marks 57% of carries and an 11% target share. Through two games snaps are Montgomery 52%, Marks 48%.
David Montgomery ranked 30th in explosive run rate and 38th in broken tackles last season.
Houston's next three opponents are the Colts, the Cowboys at home, and the Titans.
Davante Adams went 8 catches for 195 yards and 2 touchdowns (35 fantasy points) in Week 2 without Puka Nacua, and is the leading receiver in the NFL.
Matthew Stafford threw for 327 yards and 4 touchdowns in the Rams' 28-6 Week 2 win; Terrance Ferguson went 6-54 with a touchdown filling in.

Kyren Williams and Blake Corum split Week 2 almost identically: 12 carries each, 85 yards for Williams and 79 for Corum, with both involved in the receiving game; Williams caught a receiving touchdown.
Jameis Winston was 11 of 27 in relief of Jaxson Dart; Malik Nabers finished with 1 catch for 1 yard.
The league median score in the Footballers' league of record was an all-time low of roughly 91 points in Week 2, while one team scored 215 points — the highest score in league history.

Denzel Boston is 42% rostered, went 5-95 with a touchdown in Week 2, and has finished WR18 and WR11 while playing every snap and scoring in both weeks; Week 1's production was a late garbage-time 50-yard bomb touchdown, Week 2 he broke tackles.
Denzel Boston is a second-round rookie; since 2000 the only rookie wide receivers with 90%-plus snap shares and a touchdown in each of their first two games are Boston and one other.
Dontayvion Wicks went 5-74 in Week 2; his snaps went down from Week 1 but opportunities held, and his yards per route run are elite.
Emmett Johnson is 36% rostered.
Kenneth Walker is on pace for 535 opportunities through two weeks; Andy Reid said that morning they want to give Emmett Johnson more work to reduce Walker's workload.
Jonah Coleman played roughly 40% of snaps in Week 2 despite both J.K. Dobbins (injured late third quarter) and R.J. Harvey being unavailable; he out-snapped Tyler Badie in the fourth quarter.
Chuba Hubbard has finished RB10 and RB11 through two weeks with a receiving touchdown in both games.
Emanuel Wilson had 21 carries for 92 yards in Week 2; Jadarian Price has a shoulder injury and fumbled.
Kenny Gainwell scored 2 and 3 fantasy points in the first two weeks.
Tyler Shough is 48% rostered, leads the league in passing yards, is currently QB5 after two road games, and is a three-point home favorite in his home opener.
In NFL history, the only quarterbacks with 90+ attempts, 600+ passing yards and a 68% completion percentage through the first two weeks are 2015 Tom Brady and 2026 Tyler Shough.
The Saints rank number one in the NFL in pace of play under Kellen Moore.
Saints left tackle Kelvin Banks Jr. is headed to IR and will be out indefinitely — a high ankle sprain requiring surgery.
Tyler Shough had an awful first half in Week 1 under constant pressure from Aidan Hutchinson; he now faces the Raiders and Maxx Crosby.
Bryce Young is 42% rostered, ranks second in pass rate over expectation, and is averaging 8.9 yards per attempt; Carolina plays Cleveland in Week 3.
Drew Lock is the highest-rated passer in the NFL through two weeks; Jaxon Smith-Njigba has a 44% target share. A 30% target share almost guarantees a fantasy WR1 finish.
Drake Maye plays at Jacksonville in Week 3 and at Buffalo in Week 4; the Footballers would start 12 other quarterbacks over him in both.
Pittsburgh's next four opponents are Cincinnati, Cleveland, the Colts and Tampa Bay; Aaron Rodgers is top-five among quarterbacks in drops by his receivers.
Adonai Mitchell saw 12 targets and finished 6-63 in Week 2; the Jets play on the road in Detroit in Week 3.
Tre Tucker posted 3 touchdowns and 145 yards in Week 3 of last season; over four years he has produced only two or three such games per season. The Raiders play at New Orleans in Week 3.
Chris Bell played only 41% of snaps for Miami; Caleb Douglas may miss time.
Jaylen Waddle bounced back in Week 2 with double-digit targets, 8 receptions and 138 yards.

Minnesota's defense plays Tampa Bay then Miami back to back; Kansas City's defense plays Miami then Las Vegas back to back; Green Bay's defense plays Atlanta on Thursday night then Tampa Bay, with Micah Parsons coming off IR after that.
Offenses the Footballers are actively targeting for defensive streams: Miami, Tennessee, Atlanta, Washington and Cleveland.
Eli Stowers is a second-round rookie tight end currently on IR (non-injury designation), meaning he must miss four games; Philadelphia signed Zach Ertz to cover Dallas Goedert's sprained MCL.
Tucker Kraft's week-2 route participation was 84% per Fantasy Life (94% per Adam Kofler), up from 48% in week 1.
Kraft's snap count jumped from 50-something percent in week 1 to 98% in week 2.
Kraft's week 1: 3 catches for 65 yards (9.5 PPR points); week 2: 2 catches for 15 yards on 3 targets (3.5 PPR points) in an overtime game.
Green Bay gave Kraft a four-year, $75 million extension worth up to $92 million with $27 million guaranteed as signing bonus.

Sal's rest-of-season TE order entering week 2: McBride, Bowers, then Tyler Warren and Tucker Kraft in a tier of their own (Kraft TE5, moved ahead of Colston Loveland, approaching a top-60 overall player).
George Pickens has a 23% target share to CeeDee Lamb's team-leading 27%; Pickens had a 22% target share last year when he finished as a top-five fantasy WR.
Pickens through two weeks: 3 catches for 28 yards (5.8 PPR) in week 1, then 6 catches for 40 yards on 8 targets (10 points) in week 2. He was Sal's WR12 and 26th overall player entering week 2.

CeeDee Lamb went 8 catches for 145-153 yards and 2 touchdowns in week 2 at 19.1 yards per catch while Washington doubled Pickens; Schottenheimer said the Commanders' double teams on Pickens left Lamb in single coverage, and Prescott said defenses are giving Pickens a lot of attention.

Jaylen Warren in week 2 (with Rico Dowdle hurt): 11 carries for 43 yards, 2 catches for 34 yards, 72% of snaps, over 50% of rush attempts, majority of routes run, 13% target share (roughly top-10 among RBs).
Kenneth Gainwell in the Steelers offense last season: top five among RBs in receiving yards, fourth in receptions, 73 catches, 8 total touchdowns, over 1,000 total yards.
facts.about: Kenneth Gainwell (2025 comp for Jaylen Warren)

facts.fact: Jaylen Warren was Sal's 70th overall player entering week 2; Sal's free start/sit tool projects Warren 14.3 vs Quinshon Judkins 13.3 for week 3.
Matthew Golden and Christian Watson each have a 27% target share, aDOTs of 12.6 and 12.5, 33% of the team's air yards each, and 40% of end-zone targets each.

Golden's week 1: 12 targets, 6 catches, 95 yards. Week 2: 4 catches for 58 yards on 6 targets, plus two more targets that drew defensive pass interference and holding penalties downfield (per Hayden Winks), effectively 8 targets. His rookie year averaged 2 catches and 25 receiving yards per game.
Golden was Sal's 77th overall player entering week 2 and is rising into the Jameson Williams / Terry McLaurin range, above Rome Odunze.

Green Bay's WR depth behind Watson and Golden: Jayden Reed injured (back/neck, stretchered off, likely 2 to 10+ weeks), Savion Williams on IR, Skyy Moore the special-teams returner, and Bo Melton, who was a defensive back a year ago.
Emeka Egbuka leads Tampa Bay with an 18% target share; Chris Godwin is at 12% and the rookie (transcribed 'Ted Hurst') at 17% through two games.
Among the 50 WRs with 10+ targets this season, Egbuka has the worst catchable air yards rate at 39% (per Scott Barrett); no WR had a higher rate of motion at the snap than Egbuka in week 1.

Egbuka averaged 16.5 fantasy points per game over the first nine-to-ten games of his rookie year while competing with Mike Evans and a healthier Chris Godwin; he was drafted in the fourth round this year and is Sal's 42nd overall player.
Drake London last year, under then-Falcons OC Zac Robinson (now Tampa Bay's OC), played 32% of his snaps in the slot and finished with a 30% target share.
Baker Mayfield week 1: 23 of 28 (82%) with no touchdowns, Bucky Irving catching 7 of the 23 completions. Week 2: 61% completions, 5.4 yards per attempt, one interception.

Bucky Irving week 2: 17 carries for 5.2 yards per carry (to Kenny Gainwell's 2 carries), 4 catches, 77% of snaps, 54% of routes, 81% of rush attempts. Two-week totals: 70% of snaps, 69% of rush attempts, with Sean Tucker absent.
From week 12 on in 2024 (final seven games) Bucky Irving averaged 18.3 fantasy points per game and about 120 total yards per game as a top-10 RB; he is Sal's 41st overall player.

DK Metcalf has 19 targets (25% target share, top five in the NFL) and is third in the NFL in routes run at 88 (44 per week), with 2 registered drops; Aaron Rodgers has the third-most pass attempts in the NFL. Metcalf's two-week line: 4 catches for 40 yards on 10 targets, with games of 8 and 6.7 PPR points.

Javonte Williams through two weeks: over 80% of snaps in week 2, 76% of snaps and 71% of rush attempts overall; game logs of 12 carries for 41 yards and 12 for 30, saved in week 1 by a receiving touchdown.

Javonte Williams is averaging 2.96 yards per carry, 50% of his runs have gone for two or fewer yards, and he is 42nd of 43 running backs in first downs with two on 24 carries; Dallas's offensive line is dead last in yards before contact.
Dallas Pro Bowl lineman Tyler Smith is on IR with week 5 as his earliest and targeted return.

Bryce Young is the QB2 in fantasy football with three touchdowns in each of the last two weeks and only one interception; his week-1 high was 31 fantasy points on 361 passing yards against Chicago. He is at 8.9 yards per attempt and a 10.5 average depth of target, blowing away his career averages.
Carolina is playing the fastest of any team in the NFL at 23 seconds per play and ranks number one in neutral pass rate.
Bryce Young's cautionary precedent: last year in Atlanta he threw for 448 yards and three touchdowns, then followed with passing totals of 169, 206, 163, 191 and 54 yards.

Patrick Mahomes' fantasy QB finishes: QB1, QB4, QB4 pre-Nagy, then QB8, QB11, QB11 during the Matt Nagy years. This season he has six touchdowns through two weeks (one rushing and two passing in week 1 on 27 attempts for 184 yards and 20+ points, three passing in week 2 on 47 attempts).
Atlanta is the fourth team since 1978 to go its first two games without running a single play in the red zone.
In the games Drake London played with Michael Penix last year he was on pace for 180 targets and finished as the WR5 (WR1 on a week); Bijan Robinson was on pace for over 100 targets with Penix.

Vegas for Thursday Night Football: Green Bay -5.5 over Atlanta with a 43.5 total at Lambeau Field. Bills are favored by 7 over the Chargers. Bengals-Steelers in Pittsburgh has a 42.5 total, and the Carolina game also has a 42.5 total.

The Chargers are 30th in EPA per play, 30th in percentage of drives resulting in a score and 31st in turnover differential, having lost back-to-back home games 26-14; they are only the second team ever to lose consecutive home games by double digits to teams with a sub-.200 win percentage the prior year (the other: the 1926 Racine Tornadoes).
The Raiders currently rank as the number one fantasy defense through two weeks.
The last time Joe Burrow played in Pittsburgh he finished as the QB18 with one touchdown.

Green Bay's backfield: Chris Brooks leads in snaps (trusted in pass protection) and went 4 carries for 11 yards last game; both Kaleb Johnson and Marshawn Lloyd fumbled, with Johnson recovering his; Lloyd scored a receiving touchdown. A.J. Dillon had three carries for negative total yards.
Green Bay had four offensive linemen leave the week 2 game injured and internally discussed using Tucker Kraft at an offensive line position (per Graziano); one tackle went to IR.
FAAB results in the Footballers' league of record: Derrick Henry 4.65 (next-highest bid 4.51), Jeremiyah Love 3.34, Quinshon Judkins 1.56, Mike Evans 1.21.
Their league of record uses median scoring: each team plays its head-to-head opponent and also the league median that week, so up to two wins per week are available.

Excluding kneel-downs, sacks, scrambles and throwaways — plays on which skill players can't score fantasy points — the Dolphins are averaging only 46.5 plays per game, the worst full-season mark in the Fantasy Points database era; the historically bad 2025 Raiders ran about 50.
Miami is bottom-three in the NFL in yards per game through two weeks.
Defenses load the box against De'Von Achane at the third-highest rate in the NFL: 36% of his carries face a stacked front with at least one extra man.
De'Von Achane's Week 2: 20-24 carries for 74 yards (3.7 yards per carry) plus 3 catches for 19 yards, and he has not scored a touchdown yet this season.

Miami's pass-catching corps is Malik Washington (slot), rookie Caleb Douglas (foot/ankle injury, in a cast per Sal, not practicing), rookies Chris Bell and Kevin Coleman, and TE Greg Dulcich; Miami also has a defensive-minded head coach.
Kirk Cousins has more rushing attempts on the season than Malik Willis; Willis had 6 rushes for 39 yards in Week 1 and almost nothing since.

Sal's rest-of-season ordinal: De'Von Achane 30th overall, D'Andre Swift 31st, Malik Nabers 32nd, TreVeyon Henderson 61st, Josh Downs ~65th (92nd before the update), Brock Purdy 68th, Aaron Jones 93rd; Drake London 21st, George Pickens 23rd, Bijan Robinson 2nd.

Aaron Jones is about to turn 32; in Week 2 he played 80% of snaps and took 85% of the rush attempts for 23 carries, 105 rushing yards and only 10.5 fantasy points with no receiving role. Week 1 was a split: Jordan Mason 15 carries to Jones' 12.

Kevin O'Connell said Aaron Jones was sore after shouldering the Week-2 workload, and indicated Jordan Mason will be on IR about three more weeks with a fractured finger/thumb; Minnesota signed DeeJay Dallas to the active roster midweek.

Rookie Demond Claiborne played only 4% of Minnesota's snaps in Week 2 and weighs well under 200 pounds; Minnesota was down to its backup quarterback with Kyler Murray already hurt, which raised the pass-protection bar.
Aaron Jones did not practice Wednesday, then was limited Thursday (an upgrade).
TreVeyon Henderson's Week 2 debut: 16 carries for 76 yards with a 39-yard touchdown, 60% of snaps and 67% of rush attempts; excluding the long touchdown he averaged 2.7 yards per carry.

Rhamondre Stevenson played only 36% of snaps in Week 2 after an early fumble; per Ryan Heath, from that fumble to the two-minute warning the split was Henderson 76% of snaps to Stevenson 24%. Stevenson has 18 fumbles since the start of 2021, more than any other player.

Chuba Hubbard is playing 66% of Carolina's snaps and is RB8 at 17.8-19.1 fantasy points per game; Jonathon Brooks is on IR and the only other backs are A.J. Dillon and possibly Trevor Etienne if elevated. Carolina did not sign Austin Ekeler.
Only five running backs have finished top-12 in both of the first two weeks: Kenneth Walker III, Jahmyr Gibbs, Derrick Henry, Jonathan Taylor and Chuba Hubbard.
Jalen Coker leads Carolina with a 29% target share and averages 102 yards per game; Tetairoa McMillan has a 27% target share, averages 88 yards per game and has only a 59% catch rate.

Bryce Young is tied for the NFL lead with 6 passing touchdowns, has thrown 73 passes (6th-most in the league, inflated by trailing big in Week 1) and is averaging 9.8 yards per attempt against a 6.3 YPA baseline over his past two seasons; Carolina is tied for 4th in total yards per game with Baltimore.

Carolina's two opponents were the Bears (possibly a historically bad defense given preseason injuries) and the Falcons, one of the most blitz-heavy teams through two weeks with no pass rush — Aaron Rodgers also looked great against Atlanta in Week 1.
Dave Canales handed the Panthers' play-calling duties to Brad Idzik.

Stefon Diggs (32, nearly 33) leads Washington with a 24% target share while running only 60% of the routes, and leads the team by over 10 percentage points with a 31% targets-per-route-run rate; he is a top-10 fantasy WR at 16.5 points and 7.5 targets per game.
Terry McLaurin has the worst catchable-target rate in the NFL at 54%; he had a touchdown called back and a 15-20-yard catch over the middle called back in Week 2 before Jayden Daniels got hurt.
In Marcus Mariota's five starts last season, Terry McLaurin averaged 3.53 yards per route run and 14.3 fantasy points per game, finishing as WR14 over that stretch.
Marcus Mariota started eight games last season averaging 11 fantasy points, with a 23.3-point game against Denver.

Denzel Boston leads Cleveland with a 22% target share; first-round pick KC Concepcion is at 20% and Harold Fannin Jr. at 17%. Boston's production is two long touchdowns: a 46-yarder in Week 1 and a 55-yarder in Week 2 after three Buccaneers defenders missed tackles (5 catches, 95 yards on the day).

Deshaun Watson's Week 2 (24 of 30, 238 yards, 7.9 yards per attempt, 2 TDs, 80% completion) was his best game in six years with Cleveland — against a Tampa Bay defense that missed three tackles on one play.

Per Scott Barrett's targets-per-route-run and separation chart of WRs with 10-plus targets, Rashee Rice ranks at the very bottom — below Chris Godwin, Cooper Kupp and Dyami Brown — while JSN, Ladd McConkey, Amon-Ra St. Brown, Garrett Wilson, Stefon Diggs and Mike Evans grade out well.
Rashee Rice has been targeted on only 11% of his routes.

Malik Nabers was around Sal's 17th-ranked rest-of-season player heading into Week 2 with a 32% target share before re-injuring his shoulder; he fully participated in Wednesday practice and X-rays came back clean.

Jameis Winston was 11 of 27 last week (near a 30% completion rate); the Giants-Titans game has the lowest over/under of the week at 38.5 with the Giants -3, a 68% chance of rain and potentially high winds.
Cam Skattebo has seen 16 and 18 opportunities in the first two weeks as the Giants' lead back.
Matthew Golden and Christian Watson are tied for the Green Bay team-high 27% target share; Golden's Week-2 box score is understated because he drew two personal fouls.

With A.J. Terrell out for Atlanta, Matthew Golden draws mostly Mike Hughes, who ranks 89th of 128 qualifying coverage players at 1.4 yards allowed per coverage snap — the best individual matchup on the Thursday slate per Sal's matchups tool.

Tucker Kraft ran 84% of Green Bay's routes in Week 2 after about 40% in Week 1, and played 98% of snaps; Atlanta is 29th in schedule-adjusted points allowed to tight ends and already gave up production to Pat Freiermuth and Darren Waller.
Green Bay right tackle Zach Tom is out, adding to the Packers' offensive-line problems; Jayden Reed is out for Thursday.
Travis Kelce leads the Chiefs with a 25% target share, leads all NFL pass catchers in yards after the catch and leads the team in targets per route run; he is 36 and turns 37 within weeks.

Kansas City is a 10.5-point road favorite at Miami with a 46.5 total and a 28.5-point implied team total, the second-highest of the season; the Chiefs are 28-3 as double-digit favorites but have failed to cover in 55% of those games.

Brock Purdy leads all quarterbacks in EPA per play and is at an 8.9% touchdown rate (his sustainable baseline is about 7%); San Francisco is an 8.5-point home favorite against Arizona, missing Stribling, Demarcus Robinson and Christian Kirk, and possibly Mike Evans.
Deebo Samuel's alignment split is 50% out wide, 45% in the slot and 5% in the backfield.

Jared Goff threw for 327 yards and 4 touchdowns last week; he has averaged 21 fantasy points per game at home since 2022 and Detroit has the fifth-highest implied team total this week (Lions -6.5, total 47.5). The over has hit in each of Detroit's last six games.

Tyler Shough is the first player in NFL history with 3,000 passing yards and a 67% completion rate through his first 13 career games; Kellen Moore's pace gives the offense roughly five extra drop-backs — about an extra drive — per game.
Indianapolis is 30th in EPA per rush attempt and 31st in yards per carry allowed; David Montgomery had only 8 opportunities for under 5 fantasy points last week yet still out-snapped Woody Marks.

Denver is dead last in EPA per rush and dead last in yards after contact per attempt allowed, and 29th in fantasy points allowed to running backs; Blake Corum is averaging 6.0 yards per carry on 22 attempts, second only to Kenneth Walker III.

Buffalo's defense is 31st in points per drive allowed, 28th in pass success rate allowed and 30th in fantasy points allowed to wide receivers, leaking specifically to slot receivers; the Chargers-Bills line is Buffalo -7 with a 50.5 total, the second-highest of the week.

Ladd McConkey barely practiced last week and played under half the snaps as a decoy; he was a full participant on Wednesday this week. The Chargers' offense posted -0.41 EPA per play without him and +0.12 with him (cited previously), and looked significantly better with him in the first half against Arizona.

Josh Downs had 9 targets for 7 catches and 72 yards last week, holds a 30% first-read target share and 29% of the Colts' receiving yards, and averages over 10 fantasy points per game in five career games against Houston; Alec Pierce is out of the picture for at least six weeks.
Dalton Schultz went 12 catches on 14 targets for 140 yards against Cincinnati last week; Cincinnati has been the tight-end funnel to target for roughly eight straight years.

Tyler Warren led all NFL pass catchers in yards after the catch through the first three weeks of last season; his yards after catch per reception has fallen from 10.8 to 3.8, and his fantasy value is currently propped up entirely by touchdowns on about 30 receiving yards.

Dalton Kincaid was the 25th overall pick and played roughly 38% of snaps last year through a knee injury; he is now healthy, running far more routes, and has always been excellent on a per-route basis.
Harold Fannin Jr. has a 17% target share through two weeks.
Carolina is dead last in yards per carry allowed, rushing touchdowns allowed and EPA per rush this season; they were also bad last year and one of the worst run defenses of all time the year before.

Carnell Tate has a 24% target share as a rookie but has not seen a single target 20-plus yards downfield all season; Tennessee's touch distribution went 7 carries for Tony Pollard in Week 1 to 14 in Week 2, and Pollard is averaging 4.7 yards per carry.
Detroit is top-five in the league in pace of play but the Jets are so slow that the combined game pace ranks bottom-five (per Jared Smola's matchup pace data).
The Aidan Hutchinson-led Lions have the highest pressure rate in the NFL; Geno Smith's Jets have yet to commit a turnover this season.
Jameson Williams played 97% of snaps last week; Isaac TeSlaa had one more target than Williams in that game.
Adonai Mitchell is ahead of Garrett Wilson in target share.

Through two weeks Pittsburgh's defense ranks first against quarterbacks, second against wide receivers and fifth against tight ends — with the caveat that its two opponents were Cooper Rush and a struggling Drake Maye; Cincinnati is -3.5 in Pittsburgh with a 42.5 total.
Houston is -2.5 against Indianapolis with a 42.5 total; both teams are 0-2.
Carolina is -2.5 at Cleveland with a 42.5 total; Myles Garrett is no longer on the Browns.
Seattle-Washington has a 40.5 total with Seattle implied for 24 points and Washington implied for 16.8 — the lowest implied team total of the week.
The Ravens-Cowboys game carries a 52.5-point total, the biggest of the Sunday slate; it is an international game played in Brazil.
A.J. Brown's injury is a high ankle sprain that nearly required surgery, with a six-to-eight-week recovery re-reported Thursday; Sal expects five to seven more missed weeks plus a ramp-up.

Jayden Daniels' injury involves ligaments that were already torn and were not repaired; if he has surgery his season is over, and if he doesn't it is four to six weeks in a brace with a high re-injury rate. Kurt Warner said publicly he suffered the same injury in 2007 and played the next week.
Josh Jacobs is on the commissioner's exempt list facing a possible four-to-six-game suspension, with the games he has already missed counting toward it; he dealt with a groin injury in camp.
Keenan Allen's three-game suspension has been pushed, likely until after court proceedings, which probably means after the season.

Sean McVay said publicly that Puka Nacua is 'not making great progress' but that it is not a hernia and not a torn ACL; Nacua did not practice Wednesday or Thursday and has all the symptoms of a core-muscle injury without that diagnosis — surgery would mean six-plus additional weeks.
Terrance Ferguson posted 9 targets, 6 catches for 54 yards and a touchdown on 36 of 62 snaps with Nacua inactive, and Stafford threw for 327 and 4.
Davante Adams is nearly 34 years old and is Sal's WR4 for Week 3 with Nacua out.

Zay Flowers did not practice Wednesday or Thursday with a hamstring but is traveling to Brazil; the last Brazil game (Packers-Eagles) had a surface where defenders could get no grip, which is why Baltimore may protect him.

Sal's Week 3 wide receiver ranks: Christian Watson WR10, Matthew Golden WR17, Mike Evans WR22, an if-active Zay Flowers ~WR25, Xavier Worthy WR30, Adonai Mitchell WR32, with Jaylen Waddle and Ladd McConkey back-to-back.

Sal's Week 3 tight end projections: Dalton Schultz TE7 at 12.2 points, Oronde Gadsden II TE20 at 8.2, Kyle Pitts TE21 at 8.0; Travis Kelce is his TE2 and Mark Andrews would be a top-three TE if Zay Flowers is out.
Sal's start-sit tool projects Jaylen Warren 14.7 points and Aaron Jones 12.7 for Week 3, pending Rico Dowdle's status.
Jonah Coleman did not participate in Wednesday's practice while J.K. Dobbins and R.J. Harvey were limited participants; Coleman left the Week-2 game with an ankle issue but returned and scored.
Tony Pollard and Tyjae Spears both missed Wednesday practice with ankle injuries; Pollard was upgraded to limited participant Thursday.

Brock Bowers was a limited participant Wednesday and again Thursday; Travis Etienne Jr. was limited with a hamstring despite getting no work; Mike Evans and Keon Coleman did not practice Wednesday; DJ Moore was limited Wednesday but did not practice Thursday; Michael Pittman Jr. was limited and still injured; Nico Collins did not practice.

Saquon Barkley is officially limited with a stinger and is unlikely to play in Week 3; Caleb Williams is not expected to play Week 3 and Sal doubts he plays Week 4, which could leave Chicago starting a third-string quarterback against the Eagles' defensive line on Monday night.
DeVonta Smith did not practice with a hamstring — the same hamstring that cost him three weeks of training camp — though it may be a veteran rest day after a Monday night game.
Giants left tackle Andrew Thomas was downgraded on the injury report.
Mason Taylor did not practice and looks out for the Jets, opening the tight-end role for first-round rookie Kenyon Sadiq, whose PrizePicks receiving line is 25.5 yards.
David Njoku and Charlie Kolar are both on IR for the Chargers, which forces Oronde Gadsden II onto the field on nearly every play; the Chargers had been running a slow, tight-end-heavy scheme.
Darren Waller and Tetairoa McMillan carry identical 59.5-yard PrizePicks receiving projections this week; Waller's snap counts are currently very low.
Rico Dowdle still has not practiced for Pittsburgh while Jaylen Warren returned as a limited participant; DK Metcalf is listed as limited.

Michael Penix Jr. was medically cleared over a week ago but said he wasn't ready; Atlanta had acquired Tua Tagovailoa in the offseason specifically to replace him, and Tua looked worse than Penix in preseason.
Jaxson Dart is done for the season, making Jameis Winston the Giants' starter.
Patrick Mahomes' QB finishes were 1, 4, 4, 1 before Matt Nagy called the offense and 8, 11, 11 during the Nagy years; Nagy is now gone.

Sal says a fully participating practice report outweighs injury speculation: he acted on the Nabers 'fully participates' tweet plus clean X-rays rather than the pessimistic reads circulating on Twitter.

Sal's rest-of-season ordinal has Jahmyr Gibbs first, Bijan Robinson second, then Jonathan Taylor and Kenneth Walker III, with Ja'Marr Chase around fifth, Derrick Henry around 12th, Drake London 21st, George Pickens 23rd and Ashton Jeanty inside the top 15.

Both channels place Mike McDaniel as the coach controlling Oronde Gadsden II's usage on the Chargers, and both note Miami now has a defensive-minded head coach with Achane on pace for more targets since McDaniel left.
Jalen Ramsey missed Wednesday practice but was participating Thursday, which Andy called the swing factor for the Steelers' defensive matchup with Cincinnati.

Sal is publishing six YouTube videos a week this season, including a Saturday 11am news dump built off Friday practice reports, plus live streams Sunday, Monday and Thursday before kickoff that he unlists afterwards.
Detroit is a 6.5-point favorite with a 27-point implied team total and Sal projects Jahmyr Gibbs for 25.8 PPR points.
